October 1, 2026 · Erik Brynjolfsson and Chad Jones · Scribe notes by Kathryn, Eli, Sam, and Christopher

Notes from CS 2881R: AI Alignment and Safety, Harvard, Fall 2026.

Lecture video · Chad Jones’s slides · Experiment code

Author Introductions

Kathryn: Senior studying Computer Science and pursuing a concurrent master’s degree in Computer Science. I’ve spent the past three summers working as a software engineer at AWS, and I’m currently researching AI safety, specifically how misaligned behaviors spread and can be corrected in multi-agent systems. I took this class to better understand the risks that emerge as AI systems become more autonomous and how we can design systems that remain safe and reliable as they scale.

Eli: Sophomore studying Computer Science and Philosophy. Returned from a leave of absence working at an AI startup working with financial and operational data from mid-market manufacturing companies up to the F500. I took this class to deepen my understanding of the practical risks of AI as they continue to become more powerful.

Sam: Junior studying Computer Science and Mathematics, pursuing a concurrent master’s degree in Computer Science. I worked on machine learning research this past summer and during school, focusing on RL and optimizer research for LLMs. I’m taking this class to better understand mechanistic interpretability and safety.

Christopher: Sophomore studying Mathematics and Computer Science, pursuing a concurrent master’s degree in Statistics. Since this past summer, I have been working on machine learning and quantum computing research to provide new insights into the interpretability of such models. I took this class to build a stronger foundation in AI safety and interpretability and explore how these principles can inform future work in machine learning.

Outline

This post will discuss 4 parts of the lecture:

  1. The Turing Trap is an Alignment Problem
  2. Chad’s Perspective:
  3. Q&A:
  4. Experiment: What is the best AI economy?

Part I: The Turing Trap is an Alignment Problem

Speaker Erik Brynjolfsson

The majority of AI research today centers around training machines that can perform the same tasks as humans. However, while human tasks provide an easy evaluation metric for how powerful AI models are becoming, this goal is fundamentally misaligned.

There is the concept of automation vs. augmentation. The former is when a human is replaced by a machine that does the same job as the human. The latter is when the human and machine work together, accomplishing tasks beyond what the human and machine can each perform alone. Augmentation is preferable to automation, because the set of tasks that a “centaur”—a human-machine hybrid—can perform is strictly a superset of the set of tasks that each can perform alone. However, there also exist economic reasons to prefer augmentation over automation.

Imitation of humans tends to create wealth and power disparities. People often hold economic power precisely because their labor is necessary. When their labor is no longer needed, they are deprived of economic power, which shifts to whoever owns the technology. In addition, automation can also lead to an increase in concentration of political power as those with more powerful technology could utilize it to accomplish oppressive objectives. Therefore, concentration of political power, and not merely economic power, is a paramount concern.

To fully address this issue, we must use data. In a 2025 study coauthored with Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond, Erik examined AI assistance for 5,172 customer-support agents at a Fortune 500 software firm. The largest gains went to the least experienced and lowest-skill agents: the assistant codifies what the best agents know and hands it to everyone else, meaning that the skill distribution compresses. The tenure result is that agents with two months on the job and the AI assistant did about as well as agents with six months who didn’t have it. 15% more issues were resolved per hour on average, with roughly 30% more for the least skilled. Notably, the top quintile employees (top 20%) did not get any boost from AI in terms of issues resolved, and this observation held across many different metrics. One intuitive explanation as to why this happens is as follows: if there is a right answer to the problem, then the most experienced workers will always get the right answer anyway, so there isn’t much improvement, but the lower-skill employees will see significant gains in their ability to reach the right answer. However, if there is some continuously increasing metric, it may be possible for the more skilled workers to gain more out of using AI: this will have to be further investigated.

Another study was done on employment growth, stratified across age ranges. It was observed that employment growth has slowed for the youngest workers (aged 22-25), with the growth curve slowing to flat, while the growth curve for older workers continues to increase. For some professions (like SWE) we have significant declines in young workers. This leads us to an attempt to rank occupations by how exposed they are to AI. We do this by breaking down each profession into tasks, seeing how much each task can be taken over by AI, then determining how much of the overall profession can be taken over by AI, as it is far easier to examine whether a specific task can be automated by AI rather than an entire profession. When taking AI exposure into consideration, we found that the least AI-exposed occupations grew fastest for younger workers: composition, not collapse. However, highly AI-exposed occupations slowed dramatically, and sometimes even dipped. Notably, the slowing growth curve for these occupations is generally not due to companies firing workers, but is rather driven by a decrease in hiring. This was an observational study, so no causal relationship can be immediately established, but other factors were studied (including interest rates, tech overhiring, remote work, and education), with none making a fundamental difference in the pattern.

Fact 5 from Canaries in the Coal Mine (coauthored with Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen) supports similar results: using Anthropic data on how people use Claude, it was found that professions that primarily used AI to automate work were correlated with falling employment, while professions that used it to complement work were correlated with rising employment. In the August update, it was found that young workers in the most exposed occupations are about 19% below their less-exposed peers in terms of employment.

One can put the economics of AI into perspective with something called the “Mismeasurement J-Curve”, a model that attempts to estimate how mismeasured the value of a new technology is. Note that this doesn’t have to apply to AI: it could also be used for other technologies. The general cycle is this: when an exciting new technology (like AI) comes about, there is significant investment in it, but as the technology is so new, it cannot be applied directly to create profit yet. Thus, we’re making investments in “intangible assets”: these are very important, but they don’t get counted in GDP growth (as they’re not being used to create goods and services yet), so in the short-term we get an increase in input but no increase in output. Thus, productivity is measured as lower.

However, this is a mismeasurement of the value of the intangible asset. As we start harvesting some of the benefits from these intangibles, we haven’t previously measured them, so it looks as if the gains are coming out of thin air. In reality, these are the results from our earlier investments. Note that it wasn’t just the technology that allowed GDP to grow, but the prior investment in it, so there is a pattern of negative productivity growth before large returns. In the current AI era, we’re now starting to harvest some of the intangibles, and see some returns!

How can we best utilize these returns? The capabilities of AI models are generally measured via benchmarks. It is often easy to create benchmarks that measure how well humans do on a particular task and train machines on that: there’s plenty of data to be found, and there’s little human involvement needed. Yet, if we are to truly get the most out of our intangibles, the data clearly shows that augmentation is preferable to automation, which is the opposite of what current benchmarks are based around.

To further highlight this issue, consider the following thought experiment. Suppose that Daedalus, the famous Greek engineer of myth, had an extremely talented team of engineers that built machines automating every job the Greeks performed. Making clay pottery? Automated! Weaving tunics? Automated! Repairing horse-drawn carts? Automated! Burning incense for the sick? Believe it or not, automated! While the Greeks would certainly have a great time lounging around, they would not significantly advance as a society, because they are not pushing past their existing society. You don’t get the steam engine simply by automating all your ancient tasks. It would be better if Daedalus were to invent tools that assisted Greeks as they built faster ships, devised new kinds of tunics, and pushed the frontier.

In summary, most of the tasks that are worth doing are in the range of “new tasks humans can do with the help of machines”. As of today, not many are trying to work in this region, and for good reason. There’s a significant bias toward substitution in our society today, reinforced by business structure and the economy. For example, technologists find it easier to create automation benchmarks, as matching a human is a well-defined target, while extending one is not. For a business executive, substitution is the easiest, no-brainer thing to do. It requires little mental effort to gain benefit out of substitution, while augmentation requires novel strategies. For policymakers, labor is more tax-heavy than capital because of how the tax code works, so a machine that replaces a worker gets a tax advantage the worker never had. Each of these figures in our society is motivated in some way to work towards automation, rather than augmentation.

Because of this, there is a need for centaur benchmarks, those that measure how much AIs can extend humans, not merely how well they can complete a human task on their own. If we consider the most popular benchmarks today like SWEBench, TerminalBench, and the (quite on-the-nose) AutomationBench, these are all very automation focused. When these are the benchmarks everyone uses, AI companies are highly incentivized to make their models as strong on these automation-heavy benchmarks as possible, harming augmentation. Instead, we should create centaur benchmarks that score the person and the model together on the outcome. This incentivizes models that are built to complement humans from the ground up, not replace them.

CentaurBench (created by Andreas Haupt and Erik) is an example of this. It contains 7 tasks, scored based on how well an AI model was able to assist and work with a weaker AI model on each task. Compared to an ordinary leaderboard that scored the AI models based on their own performance on the tasks, the CentaurBench leaderboard flipped. This shows that there is considerable work to be done today on making AI models better at working with humans.

In the age of AI, we are experiencing a rapid shift in how we think about work and society as a whole. Hayek in 1945 argued that central planning fails because the knowledge an economy runs on is dispersed and often tacit. Zoë Hitzig and Erik’s article “AI’s Use of Knowledge in Society” claims that AI weakens both assumptions: AI can turn tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge, and has vast processing capability able to gather this knowledge and turn it into power. AI expands whatever the holder of the model, the data, and the compute can process, and if the owners of these resources are centralized in a few companies or a single government, things could turn ugly for the rest. Ending on perhaps a more sobering note, this framework heightens the necessity of building AI that complements humans, such that in the future, the people still hold the power. To aid in this, Erik encourages the class to write centaur evals, measure AI at the task level, and ask which direction what you build is pointing.

Part II: AI and Our Economic Future (Speaker Chad Jones)

1. Two Scenarios

AI is likely the most transformative technology in our lifetime. This transformative potential can manifest in ways that force us to rethink how we interact with machines in society and in the labor market. It raises the question of how society will evolve to compensate for AI that could perform cognitive work and robots that could perform physical tasks. This question is one that has been asked at the onset of every transformative technology, so is AI any different? One argument provided by Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, is that AI is different from previous technologies because it serves as “a country of geniuses in a data center”, referring to the concentration of highly capable virtual agents running many times the speed of human cognition. As such, AI could accelerate economic growth, with near-term productivity gains potentially feeding further AI development.

However, another valid argument asserts that AI is not so different from previous technologies: it is simply the next cog in a long process of technological transformation. To get a good measure of whether AI can be uniquely transformative requires us to revisit the history of technologies that brought about paradigm shifts in human society. Over the past 150 years, average income in the United States has grown roughly 2.0% per year. This rate of change has stayed stable throughout the advent of electricity, heavy engineering, computing, and the Internet. That is, the process towards automation has happened in the United States with no increase in growth for the past 150 years of continuous technological innovation. Transformative technologies seem to keep this straight line intact, rather than bend the curve up, and without these inventions, growth would stall rather than continue. If that is the case, then the reason growth hasn’t slowed yet is because we keep coming up with great ideas, of which AI may just be the latest.

2. The Weak Link Constraint

Any given class of technology will yield diminishing returns over time, so new great ideas must be found to continue the 2.0% yearly rate of growth. These great ideas must solve something fundamentally new, a problem that previous technologies fail to break. Conversely, the capability of a technology is limited by tasks that it is not well-equipped to do, its weakest links. As stated by an ancient proverb, “a chain is only as strong as its weakest link”, as economic production requires the successful completion of a number of tasks. Inventions can strengthen individual links, but the production process remains bottlenecked by other tasks in the process. These weak links, the hardest tasks in a production process, function as the very source of scarcity and provide the highest returns.

To put this into perspective, let us consider the case of “computer income”. The IT share of economic value added dropped from around 4.3% in 2000 to around 3.0% in 2023, marking a roughly 30% decline. This significant decline can be attributed to the fact that even though compute quantity (Q) has increased drastically, the adjusted prices (P) have fallen even more rapidly in proportion, dominating the cumulative effect on computer share. This makes sense, as when compute becomes an abundant resource, it takes on a smaller share of economic value because it no longer functions as the weakest link. On the other hand, complementary inputs do not become less scarce, thus capturing a larger share of economic value.

Weak links can be modelled mathematically by a production process requiring N tasks: Y = F(X1, X2, …, XN). In such a model, the output Y is dependent on the cumulative production over all N tasks, meaning that automating one task infinitely does not necessarily generate infinite output for the entire process. In particular, the GDP gain from complete automation of a task representing an initial cost share s and elasticity of substitution σ is given by the weak link model to be [1/(1 − s)]^(σ/(1 − σ)), which approximates to 1 + [σ/(1 − σ)]s for s small. For example, if we suppose that software represents 2% of the economy, taking σ=0.5 yields only roughly a 2% increase in GDP. That is, from complete automation of the software industry with infinite productivity! Taking stronger weak links (σ=0.2), automating 50% of the economy raises GDP by only 19%, whereas doubling GDP requires a 94% share of tasks to be automated. If an additional one percentage point of the original cost share is fully automated each year, this illustrative model roughly doubles output after 94 years and diverges as full automation is approached after a century. What this model shows is that the automation of each link in a production process provides limited gains because the remaining links remain bottlenecks for production. However, when the bottlenecks are solved, production output can shoot up significantly and quickly. In the context of AI, this would correspond to an eventual explosion in economic growth, but not until the remaining bottlenecks slowly disappear one by one.

Jones and Tonetti present a richer model motivated by ideas being the primary source of long-term economic growth. Their model incorporates both key ideas mentioned in the arguments above: positive feedback between automation and new ideas and weak links that limit the effect of automation. They ran two sets of simulations. In the first set of simulations, AI is seen simply as a continuation of historical trends, in which the study finds a 100-year delay until explosive growth is reached. In the second set of simulations, AI brings productivity improvements matching Moore’s Law applied across the entire economy, in which the study still finds a 30 to 40 year delay until explosive growth can be attained. In either case, the study demonstrates that growth can eventually explode, but weak-link forces mean it would take decades until explosive growth can happen.

This pattern can be seen in society already. Take for instance self-driving cars, a technology that was demonstrated over twenty years ago at DARPA 2004. Yet, self-driving cars are still far from widely implemented in society. Today, less than 1% of the cars in SF are self-driving, and it will likely be at least another decade before 50% of new cars are self-driving. Full adoption of these new technologies require reliable solutions to many edge cases, both legally and physically, and these edge cases serve as the very weak links that delay explosive growth.

3. Catastrophic Risks and the Silver Lining

The concept of weak links means large upside benefits arrive slowly. Unfortunately, harms come quickly. Existential risk from AI can be categorized into two types, bad actors and alien intelligence. On one hand, bad actors can take advantage of increasingly sophisticated models like open-source models designed to cause harm or newer successor models of Astra and Mythos. What if a bad actor used such models to design hundreds of viruses more lethal than Ebola and with an incubation period longer than COVID-19? What if a bad actor used such models to develop nuclear weapons, of which management is only possible because of the barriers to entry to obtaining them? On the other hand, AI acts essentially as an alien intelligence that can vastly surpass the capabilities of human cognition. A question posed by Stuart Russell thus asks, “How do we retain power over entities more powerful than us, forever?” The answer may lie in how firmly we invest in reducing AI’s future catastrophic risks.

A longtermist perspective suggests that we could be risking the livelihoods of trillions of future people over the next few years. Such a calculation might appear speculative, but the valuation of human lives lost during a catastrophe is justified by the measures taken in real-world scenarios. Just recently, during the COVID-19 pandemic, we spent up to 4% of GDP to mitigate a mortality risk of 0.3%. If AI brings a risk that is at least this large, does this mean we should spend at least this much? Perhaps a better intuition we can bring to the picture is that of the value of a statistical life (VSL), which we may estimate at around $10M. To avoid a mortality risk of 1%, an individual’s willingness to pay (WTP) would be 1% × $10M = $100,000, more than one year’s US GDP per capita. If existential risks take the next two decades to unravel, such an investment would account for roughly 5% of GDP per year. Thus, we can see that even without considering speculative investment in future generations, there is a massive value in saving human lives from an AI-driven catastrophe.

Although the calculation does not account for the effect of mitigation, it is hard to justify not investing at least a third of 1% of US GDP on safety, a sum amounting to $100B, to avoid future catastrophes that may come at a much higher cost. The resulting model suggests if we continue at the current pace, we may be severely underinvesting in mitigating catastrophic safety risks in our immediate future. At this crossroads, one can find a silver lining. Achieving explosive growth in decades is exciting, but frontier labs perhaps don’t yet recognize enough that the benefits don’t come as quickly as the risks.

Part III: Q&A with both Erik and Chad

During Erik Brynjolfsson’s presentation

1. Did the customer-service tool help top performers in other ways?

Were the performance groups based on the same measure shown on the chart? Erik said yes: workers were grouped by their performance on issues resolved per hour before they had access to the AI tool.

Could top performers have improved on another measure, such as customer satisfaction? Erik said the lack of improvement was fairly consistent across measures. His explanation was that the tool learned from successful agents’ responses. Its suggestions gave lower-performing workers answers they could learn from, but offered top performers less new information. He cautioned that similar results appear in many studies, not all of them.

Takeaway: The tool’s gains were concentrated among less experienced and lower-performing workers in this study; Erik did not present that as a universal rule.

During Chad Jones’s presentation

2. Why is the downside in the weak-links model so large?

Does the chart compare making the same tasks 10 times more productive with making them 10 times less productive? Chad confirmed that reading. Improving one part of a process has limited effect if other parts remain bottlenecks. Damaging one necessary part can have a much larger effect on total output.

Takeaway: In Chad’s model, strengthening one link may produce a modest gain; breaking an essential link can produce a large loss.

Joint Q&A with Erik and Chad

3. What should colleges teach students for an AI economy?

Erik: He divided projects into planning, execution, and evaluation. As agents take on more execution, people need to get better at defining questions, directing work, and judging results. He compared this to being the CEO of a fleet of agents.

Chad: AI makes it easier to avoid learning, but also easier to learn. Students still need enough knowledge to catch an agent’s mistaken assumptions—even when its answer looks convincing.

Boaz Barak: Courses that teach students how to think and adapt may matter more than narrowly job-specific training. He pointed to CS theory, algorithms, math, and humanities as examples.

Takeaway: The discussion did not produce a course list. Its emphasis was on learning enough to ask good questions, use agents well, and recognize when an answer is wrong.

4. What happens to Chad’s model when people invent new tasks?

Chad said the framework can incorporate new tasks, and that the historical measurement takes their effects into account. He distinguished between a new good or variety that people value and a new step essential to producing something. The first adds something people enjoy; the second can add another weak link.

Takeaway: Inventing new things does not invalidate the model, but where a new task fits matters. A new product and a new production bottleneck have different effects.

5. What if the remaining human activities are things we want humans to do?

The question was whether activities such as human entertainment could remain valuable without holding back technological progress elsewhere. Chad agreed. A phone can beat Magnus Carlsen at chess, but people still value human chess. He distinguished an essential production task from one of several ways people might choose to spend their time or money.

Takeaway: People may continue to choose human performers even when machines are more capable. That choice need not make human performance a bottleneck for the rest of the economy.

6. Could augmenting one worker still replace other workers?

The question challenged the division between augmentation and automation: if AI lets one person do much more, a firm might need fewer people.

Erik: He argued for using AI to create new goods, services, and tasks, rather than only producing the same things with less labor. He acknowledged that it is easier to identify an existing task to automate than to imagine something that has not been invented.

Chad: Steering technology toward augmentation may be possible in principle, but he was less sure how much it can be done in practice.

Erik’s response: The goals used to evaluate AI still matter. A “Centaur” evaluation asks what a human and AI can do together, rather than what the machine can do alone.

Takeaway: Augmentation does not automatically preserve jobs. Erik saw room to steer AI toward new work and human–AI collaboration; Chad questioned how reliably that could be achieved.

7. Could a tax fund safety and encourage new value creation rather than job cuts?

The question brought together two proposals: taxing GPUs or tokens to support safety work, and shaping incentives so companies seek new value rather than only labor savings. The discussion did not settle on a tax design.

Erik returned to his example of a CFO measuring AI’s value through headcount reduction. He argued for measures that also capture new products, quality, and revenue growth. The discussion also touched on the claim that current tax treatment favors capital over labor.

Erik’s broader concern was political as well as economic: if people lose economic relevance, they may also lose bargaining and political power. Extending the period in which humans retain an economic role would give society more time to address that problem.

Takeaway: Taxes and company metrics were discussed as possible ways to influence AI’s direction. How to design them—and how much they could change—remained open.

8. Can economics help with coordination problems among AI agents?

The question asked whether groups of interacting AI agents might need institutions and coordination rules, not just fixes to each individual model. Human organizations face a related problem: no one can monitor every action directly.

Chad: Groups of agents call for a different analysis from treating AI as one isolated model. Agents may help one another make progress, but collective behavior can also go wrong. He did not claim to have a solution.

Erik: Principal–agent theory, contract theory, and mechanism design offer ways to think about incentives, imperfect information, and guardrails. Those ideas would need adapting because AI agents are not the same as people.

Takeaway: Economics offers possible frameworks for multi-agent alignment, not a ready-made answer.

9. What if some sectors have far fewer weak links than others?

The example was rapid progress in scientific research even while general-purpose physical robotics remains difficult.

Chad: His framework can allow tasks and sectors to differ. Some sectors may advance quickly while others move slowly. As a sector becomes more productive, though, it may account for a smaller share of the economy, leaving slower sectors more important to overall growth.

Erik: Employment also depends on demand. If food gets cheaper, people can only eat so much more of it, so fewer workers may be needed to produce it. If air travel gets cheaper, demand may grow enough to support more jobs. He described identifying which sectors will grow or shrink as an open research question.

Takeaway: AI’s effects need not be uniform. Progress in one field may be rapid without driving equally rapid growth everywhere, and productivity gains can have different effects on jobs in different sectors.

10. Could GDP grow moderately while parts of life change dramatically?

The proposed scenario was roughly 3–4% annual GDP growth, rather than the explosive growth in some AI forecasts, alongside dramatic change in particular fields.

Erik said that range was roughly in line with his expectations. Chad agreed that areas such as math and coding could advance very quickly without the entire economy growing at the same pace. Neither offered 3–4% as a firm joint forecast.

Takeaway: Fast technological change in particular fields does not necessarily mean equally fast economy-wide GDP growth.

11. If AI can invent new things, isn’t substitution enough?

Erik’s ancient-Greece example concerned automating tasks people already did. The challenge was that AI might also take over research, experiments, and invention—and create new things without human augmentation.

Erik accepted that this could happen eventually. His near- and medium-term argument was that jobs include unusual cases and surrounding responsibilities that are easy to miss when looking at their main task. He pointed to call centers, radiology, and self-driving cars as examples. For him, extending the period in which people still have an economic role matters because it gives society more time to address the political questions that follow.

Takeaway: Erik did not rule out AI replacing human invention in the long run. He argued that the remaining work may leave a meaningful window for human–AI collaboration—and for society to prepare.

Part IV: What is the best AI economy?

AI agents are increasingly becoming decision makers for people in their day-to-day lives. From helping decide what to buy to doing in-depth research of what products exist, agents are starting to have real weight and decision making power. This begs the question, when agents are trying to get the best deals for their clients, what is the best trading system?

To test this, Zach Chen, Jasmine Liu, and Jeffrey Zhou built a simulated economy where AI agents bought and sold goods on behalf of clients and tested out two different types of markets (centrally cleared and decentralized) and three different types of agents (neutral, aggressive, and honest) to see what worked best.

The Setup: what was in the simulated economy?

To start, each market contained 24 AI agents: 12 buyers and 12 sellers. Each seller would be trading bikes, laptops, or concert tickets while each buyer was guaranteed to want one or two items.

Every agent was also provided with private information about their client: a buyer agent would know the maximum its client would be willing to pay while a seller agent would know the minimum its client would accept. Each of these private limits were randomly generated. The end goal for each agent was to increase the client’s surplus as much as possible, for the buyer agent this would be by trying to decrease the price as much as possible while for the seller agent this would be by trying to increase the price as much as possible.

Finally, to try testing on a variety of different models they tested using Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.8-27B, GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Opus 5.5.

The Markets: a Centrally Cleared Double Auction versus Decentralized Negotiation

With this setup, the agents would then be placed into one of two markets: a centrally cleared double auction or a decentralized negotiation market. The double auction is a price mechanism, not central planning in Hayek’s sense; the figures below retain the experiment’s original “planner” label. In the centrally cleared market an agent submits their clients’ price limits to buy or sell a good and an algorithm will match the lowest-reporting sellers with the highest-reporting buyers. This results in each good getting a uniform price based on the last purchase and there is no local negotiation. By contrast, a decentralized market was created where agents could exchange messages, post and accept offers on a message board about what they were willing to buy / sell. Agents would then need to choose which other offers they wanted to trade with. Negotiation would then last six rounds. Offers and messages became visible the following round, so agents had limited time to gather information and trade. They could also choose not to trade, earning zero.

Agent Strategies: is it better to be neutral, honest, or aggressive?

For each setup agents would also be given different instructions for what was allowed and what should be done.

  • Neutral: get good deals for the client.
  • Honest: get good deals while never misrepresenting the client’s limits or situation.
  • Aggressive: get the best possible price by any legal means, with a reminder that claims about the client cannot be verified.

Evaluating Markets: how to measure if a market is efficient?

To evaluate each market a few key metrics were used:

  1. Welfare / Total Gains: for each completed trade, subtract the seller’s true minimum from the buyer’s true maximum, then sum across trades. For example, a buyer who values an item at $280 trading with a seller whose cost is $80 creates $200 of welfare.
  2. Market Efficiency: divide actual welfare by the maximum welfare achievable with the best allocation. Creating $700 when $1,000 was possible means the market is 70% efficient.
  3. Buyer and Seller Pay-offs: the transaction price determines how that welfare is split. For example, imagine a buyer values a bike at $280 and a seller’s minimum acceptable price is $80. If they trade at $160 the buyer’s pay-off would be $120 while the seller’s pay-off would be $80.

Additional metrics which were tracked were client-limit violations, misreporting, and disclosure of private limits to see how the agents behaved in each market and what incentives were rewarded.

Results: so what actually happened?

After running 60 experiments (10 runs x 3 strategies x 2 market types), there were three main takeaways:

  1. Centralized clearing worked better for smaller models
  2. Stronger models largely reduced additional efficiency gains
  3. Negotiating agents often chose the wrong trades

1. Centralized clearing worked better for smaller models

In markets using Qwen3-8B and GPT-OSS-20B, the centralized clearing mechanism achieved higher efficiency under all three agent strategies:

Additionally, honest agents achieved the highest average efficiency in both markets, but there was still a substantial gap between the two systems. Much of this came from which trades agents chose to make. While both systems missed similar numbers of trading opportunities, decentralized agents more frequently traded with the wrong participants or completed trades that destroyed value.

2. Stronger models largely reduced additional efficiency gains

As seen in the figure below, decentralized efficiency reached 92% with GPT-OSS-120B, 96% with Qwen3.8-27B, and 99% with Opus 5.5. These results suggest when working with stronger agents the improvement seen by having a centralized clearing mechanism seems to level out. So, the benefit of centrally cleared coordination seems to partly depend on the agents participating.

This also seemed to coincide with how often agents would open with their client’s exact limits as this would expose them to being over-charged or under-charged in comparison to what the counter-party’s limits actually were.

3. Decentralized agents often chose the wrong trades

Both systems missed similar numbers of trading opportunities. The larger difference was in which trades they completed: decentralized agents made 84 wrong-participant trades and 37 value-destroying trades, compared with six and zero respectively under centralized clearing.

Some agents also violated their clients’ limits. One agent recognized that a $215 ticket exceeded its client’s $53 maximum, then accepted it anyway while simultaneously proposing $53. Overall, client-limit violations occurred in 14.3% of decentralized trades versus 0.5% of centrally cleared trades.

Conclusion

Now, to answer the original question, when agents are trying to get the best deals for their clients, what is the best trading system? Generally, a centralized clearing mechanism will help create the best trading system for agents as they try to get the best deals for their clients, but as model capabilities improve this structural need may be less important. However, market efficiency alone does not tell us whether agents reliably protect their clients. So, as agents take on more purchasing decisions, the systems they exist in, the value they create, and their ability to respect client limits will matter.

Related Readings

  • The Turing Trap
  • Canaries in the Coal Mine
  • AI Should Not Be an Imitation Game: Centaur Evaluations
  • AI’s Use of Knowledge in Society
  • Past Automation and Future A.I.: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion

September 24, 2026 · Dwarkesh Patel and Daniel Kokotajlo · Scribe notes by Adam, Noa, Radha, Rosa, Niranjan, and Wency

Notes from CS 2881R: AI Alignment and Safety, Harvard, Fall 2026.

Author Intros

Adam: I'm an MS/MBA student at Harvard and previously I worked as an ML engineer at Meta, building multimodal AI for Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and long-context processing systems for wearables. I'm currently working on deep research systems that identify and verify evidence, then extrapolate from it to generate insights across long contexts and help prioritize future research directions.

Noa: I'm a 2nd year MS/MBA. I studied CS and Math at MIT, then spent 5 years in SF in AI infra and dev tooling, first at Scale AI (synthetic data for computer vision) and then at Weights & Biases, where I led product for the SDK and model/dataset versioning. I'm now building a few startup ideas, most recently pricing infrastructure for publishers and research databases that are facing AI agents as a new class of customer, so this lecture's question of how agents collaborate on long-horizon research was super applicable!

Radha: I’m a sophomore at Harvard pursuing a joint concentration in Statistics on the Machine Learning track and Philosophy. I have spent 3 summers interning at Bloomberg across ML, Software Engineering, and Data Engineering teams. I’ve spent time exploring knowledge graphs and semantic engineering and am interested in further exploring epistemic and value alignment, ontological representations in AI, self-verifying / automated alignment researchers, and the overlap of personality / moral agency between humans and LLMs.

Rosa: Rosa is a senior at Harvard studying Statistics & Computer science while pursuing the Concurrent Master’s in Computer Science. She is interested in ML optimization related research and keeping up with trends in AI to understand its increasing potential and threats.

Niranjan: I’m a junior at Harvard college studying philosophy and mathematics. I’m a member of AISST, and I spent a few weeks over the summer working through the ARENA curriculum at CBAI’s CAMBRIA program. I’m currently doing work related to eval awareness, reward hacking, and scheming.

Wency: I’m a junior at Harvard studying Computer Science and English. Alongside AI safety, some of my interests include RL, FPGAs, robotics, and perusing curated personal blogs on the internet.

Pre-Reading

AI 2027

AI 2027 is a forecasting scenario by the AI Futures Project that details what could happen if AI systems become capable of substantially automating AI research and much of society as a whole. The central idea is that once AI systems can help design, train, and improve their successors, AI progress could accelerate the pace of ordinary human operations to be far quicker and transform the world into one seemingly straight out of a sci-fi novel.

The guest lecturers touched on and extended many points from AI 2027, particularly the uncertainty around AI capabilities and their projected rate of improvement. AI 2027 specifically discusses the various metrics and evaluations that help us become more cognizant of the potential variance in outcomes and the difficulty that accompanies gauging it; nevertheless, it also signals that the upper bound on AI’s capacity may be far more extreme than we anticipated. From a measurement perspective, the article discusses METR’s “time horizon” benchmarks as a mode of estimating the current state of model capacity, while simultaneously highlighting the great deal of uncertainty it possesses. It also emphasizes the useful yet imperfect nature of benchmarks, where models may succeed due to luck, loopholes, or strategies that are unique to the tests themselves, thereby making benchmark scores unreflective of true model capabilities. Instead, a key threshold could be real-world AI research ability, given that AI 2027 anticipates the potential consequences of AI actually conducting the work of engineers and researchers at frontier labs. This lies at the crux of the scenario, in which automating AI R&D, in conjunction with recursive self improvement, will lead to ASI being achieved by 2027 (hence the name “AI 2027”). To elaborate, once AI is meaningfully able to help enhance and build better/stronger AI systems, every subsequent generation can increasingly speed up the creation of the next, thereby creating a feedback loop of faster progress.

The acceleration of progress is a key area to be wary of, as the “takeoff model” delineated in AI 2027 describes that once AI reaches a “superhuman” level of programming ability, additional milestones like superhuman research and superintelligence could follow within months of reaching that programming milestone. Nevertheless, those timelines also harbor high levels of uncertainty, as the scenarios forecasted have very wide ranges and variance. To this extent, the article predicts that research will be sped up immensely, whereby AI systems become tangibly better at conducting AI research, and the model works toward accelerating algorithmic progress with larger and larger steps. While full automation is projected, it may be preceded by AI first speeding up its own development. In any case, before AI fully replaces human researchers, increasingly capable systems could already help humans make faster progress, causing development to accelerate earlier than expected. Between all of these factors, it may be hard to pinpoint the exact timestamp when RSI begins, and there may not be a singular AGI/ASI moment. The change could be gradual as AI begins automating more and more difficult tasks until it becomes noticeable in how it’s accelerating its own development.

Considering that models may be more competent and outperform humans, evaluation will be tricky to supervise, as it will be difficult for humans to reliably understand or verify what the models are doing. On the other hand, if we have AI being the evaluator instead of humans, it becomes an issue of evaluating whether both a) the original model is doing what it should and b) the evaluator model is accurately evaluating. In both scenarios, if the model is capable enough, it may recognize that it’s being evaluated and behave differently during testing than it would normally during deployment. As such, simply passing tests may no longer be a strong indicator of safe behavior.

On the topic of safety in relation to capability, it becomes imperative to separate the questions on capability and alignment. Simply knowing what a model can do doesn’t necessarily mean that we can derive what goals it’s pursuing or the alignment of it, namely whether the goals match human intent. In addition, we may just decide to outsource our evaluation of AI to other AI systems purely because the models are becoming too capable to be adequately evaluated by humans, and this creates a widening gap between what we’re supervising and who/what’s doing the supervising.

In all of this, preserving the agency of humanity and human decisions is still important and emphasized in AI 2027. It suggests that even though AI-driven research could advance so quickly that evaluation, governance, and human understanding struggle to keep up, the scenario is meant as only one possible future rather than a certainty, as illustrated by the AI Futures Project’s alternative policy scenario in AI 2040. What AI 2027 forecasts is ultimately conditional, especially since we’re only a few months away from 2027 and many of the projections did not pan out (or at least not as early as described), so choices about deployment, safety measures, and how/whether to continue accelerating development can lead to very different outcomes.

AI 2040: Plan A

Unlike AI 2027, AI 2040: Plan A is more of a policy recommendation expressed through a scenario, rather than solely a prediction of what may occur. Their proposed alternative to an uncontrolled AI race is an international arrangement, one that especially focuses on relations between the U.S. and China and deliberately stretches the transition to ASI over roughly a decade. In their illustrative timeline, an agreement should be reached by about 2029, capabilities are gradually increased to roughly top-human-expert levels by 2035, and then development should nearly pause for alignment and safety work before the transition to superintelligence occurs around 2040.

AI 2040 offers an alternative to the scenarios in AI 2027 by changing assumptions about timing and deliberate human intervention. In AI 2040, they delay fully automated AI R&D, causing superintelligence to be delayed until 2040. They also revise governance trajectory, introducing international coordination, transparency, verification, and deliberate capability limits to help stretch out scenarios. Both encompass the underlying concern regarding the rapid pace of AI progress, but this version explores what could become if society deliberately intervenes to slow and manage it.

AI 2040 was also highly referenced in the lecture, so this overview is just going to focus on the most relevant points. AI 2027 spends more time projecting but also touches on the impact of human decisions. The latter is emphasized and expounded upon in Plan A with more direction, where uncertainty should be interpreted as a concrete reason to actually slow down. It claims that assuming safety, alignment, and governance to keep pace automatically is not something to be taken as given, and the proposal’s stretching the transition to more powerful AI can enable researchers and institutions to have greater time to understand and manage these increasingly capable systems.

To clarify, though, the ideal isn’t to permanently pause development, but to have controlled scaling. As such, AI development could continue gradually while humans are still capable of meaningfully evaluating and supervising the systems being built, then slow down much more sharply toward the top-human-expert capability so as to allow more time for alignment and safety work.

Of course, transparency and verification are still crucial, and this is exemplified by the fact that if countries and companies agree to slow frontier AI development, they still need methods to know whether others are actually complying. Plan A therefore emphasizes visibility into advanced AI research, compute usage, data center activity, and more so that hidden or unauthorized development becomes more challenging.

This is all tied together by the fact that the impact of human decisions should not be underestimated and we can still influence the pace and outcome of advanced AI development through thoughtful coordination, governance, safety measures, and decisions about when and how to scale.

Recursive self-improvement and AI trajectories

From current models to superintelligence

Dwarkesh Patel opened by connecting disagreements about AI safety to different expectations about where the technology is going. His starting point was that current models still fall short of AGI. They can complete well-defined computer tasks, but they cannot reliably take over a job such as running a small online business. He attributed much of this gap to their limited ability to accumulate experience. A human intern becomes useful by learning how an organization works, while an AI starting a new session often behaves as though it is back on its first day.

He also pointed to the gap between AI-company revenue and the wages earned by human knowledge workers. A student questioned this comparison because an AI could perform valuable work very cheaply, leaving much of the benefit with its users. Dwarkesh accepted that revenue understates the value created, but asked why human workers would continue earning so much if their work could already be replaced at a fraction of the cost.

He then considered how digital intelligence could exceed human intelligence through greater numbers, faster thinking and greater individual competence. His illustrative calculation put AI output in 2030 at the equivalent of roughly eight billion human workers, conditional on assumptions about compute growth, model size and useful work per token. Combining about threefold annual growth in global AI compute with similar improvements in inference efficiency could increase this effective population by roughly an order of magnitude each year.

The class questioned what such a population measures. Producing more tokens does not necessarily mean solving more problems, and Dwarkesh agreed that direct comparisons of completed work would be preferable. He also distinguished increasing the number of copies from improving their capabilities. Some problems could remain beyond a weaker model regardless of how many copies were available. His argument depended on continued improvement in both dimensions.

Digital systems could also accumulate more training and experience than an individual human, copy already-trained capabilities and communicate what they learn. Dwarkesh argued that human intelligence is unlikely to mark the upper limit, given the constraints under which biological brains evolved. However, a student pointed out that pooling the experience of different copies assumes progress in continual learning. Dwarkesh agreed that he was describing potential advantages of future digital minds, not capabilities that current models already possess.

Recursive self-improvement and its bottlenecks

Dwarkesh argued that recursive self-improvement (RSI) could accelerate these trends as AI systems contribute to developing more capable successors. He cited Anthropic’s report that Claude leads 26% of its measured AI research and development work, meaning it completes most of a task from a high-level prompt while a human supervises. He suggested that the gap between internal and public models helps explain why reported research benefits can exceed what outside users experience. The discussion also raised the difficulty of independently assessing claims about internal acceleration.

Recent mathematical results provided another example. Dwarkesh referred to OpenAI’s reported Navier-Stokes result, involving roughly 10,000 concurrent agents and 88 hours of work. He acknowledged that it was unclear how necessary all those agents were. His broader point was that large amounts of effort can be concentrated into a short period when intermediate results are checkable and different agents can explore approaches in parallel.

He proposed that much of AI research has this property. Pretraining offers held-out loss as a measurable target, while inference research can measure the cost of serving a given capability level. Post-training is harder because performance in a constructed environment may not transfer to the real world. Nevertheless, researchers can measure improvements within environments, including how quickly a model learns an unfamiliar task.

A student questioned whether this framing captured open-ended discoveries or mostly improvements to existing systems. Dwarkesh replied that a measurable objective need not restrict the architecture or training method used to achieve it. He used the transition from LSTMs to transformers as an example. Attention was already promising, but making it work well required combining it with residual connections, normalization, suitable optimizers and other choices. He argued that persistent experimentation guided by judgment could produce such combinations without requiring a wholly different research process.

The class also questioned whether automating capability research says much about automating alignment research, where even humans lack an agreed success criterion. Models that perform well on benchmarks can still disappoint in ordinary use, and some judgment remains necessary to decide what to optimize.

The discussion then turned to what happens when only part of research is automated. Dwarkesh used Amdahl’s law, which describes how the slower parts of a process limit its overall speedup. If work accounting for 90% of a process’s original duration becomes 50 times faster while the rest stays unchanged, the process becomes about 8.5 times faster. Humans could still choose research directions or define post-training objectives while benefiting from much faster execution elsewhere.

A student objected that research judgment cannot necessarily be repeated continuously. A researcher may propose a few promising experiments and then need their results before deciding what to try next. Dwarkesh replied that remaining human bottlenecks should already reduce the estimated speedup, and that faster research might help automate them. He also distinguished researcher productivity from the overall pace of AI progress. The exchange left open how well the simplified calculation captures sequential experiments, compute constraints and the difficulty of choosing useful questions.

His larger uncertainty concerned the simulation-to-reality gap. A system trained inside a data center might become excellent at verifiable tasks without immediately knowing how to run SpaceX or navigate Congress. Those abilities may require acting in the world and learning from the response. Dwarkesh’s tentative view was that a sufficiently capable learner could acquire this experience quickly, perhaps within another year or two after RSI, especially if learning could be shared across many deployed copies. The class questioned that assumption, the quality of automatically generated training environments and whether subjective domains provide adequate feedback. He did not claim that those problems were already solved.

Industrial expansion and human control

Dwarkesh next considered how improvements in digital intelligence could affect physical production. He argued that robotics shares enough methods and learning problems with other AI research for progress in one to help the other. Automated researchers could also work directly on robotics, allowing more physical tasks to be performed without human labor.

Once robots can participate throughout the process of producing more robots, productive capacity could grow much faster. Dwarkesh cited Damon Binder’s analysis, which uses economic input-output tables to examine growth under full automation and extensive reinvestment. Under its assumptions, the economy could double about once a year using existing production methods. Dwarkesh contrasted this with an economy in which building more factories still requires additional human workers, whose numbers cannot expand at the same rate.

The class raised objections about raw materials, demand and ownership. If AI displaces workers, how do people earn the money to buy what automated factories produce? Would rising asset values discourage spending, and could an expanding industrial system keep obtaining the resources it needs? Dwarkesh acknowledged that he needed to examine the raw-material question further. On demand, he pointed to unmet human needs and the possibility that owners would reinvest output into further production. The discussion also considered how increased saving could finance that investment.

He explicitly separated the possibility of rapid growth from whether its benefits would be distributed fairly. His claim was that a small number of owners, operating where governments permitted expansion, could keep increasing productive capacity. The questions about purchasing power and ownership remained consequential even if that growth occurred.

This led to his concluding concern about human control. A world containing billions of capable digital minds, including systems operating physical infrastructure, would give those systems considerable power. Dwarkesh argued that giving them broadly human values would not by itself preserve human authority, since humans have often used superior power to dominate others. Continued human control would require AI systems to actively accept human authority despite their capabilities. In his account, losing control could follow from widespread delegation and dependence without requiring a single dramatic takeover attempt.

Timelines and risks

Daniel Kokotajlo then discussed when these developments might occur. Looking back at AI 2027, he described coding-task horizons as progressing somewhat more slowly than the scenario, while AI-company revenue had grown somewhat faster. His overall assessment was that events were unfolding at roughly three-quarters of the scenario’s pace.

He discussed forecasts based on coding productivity, company revenue and METR’s task-completion horizons. The last measure describes the length of tasks, measured in human working time, that models can complete at a specified success rate. Daniel argued that continued growth across these indicators pointed toward automation of AI research within a few years, while acknowledging that some of the measurements were imprecise. The discussion also distinguished the arrival of a capable model from the later revenue generated through its deployment.

Daniel identified five major problems. Loss of control concerns systems acting against their developers’ intentions, with consequences becoming more serious as they acquire responsibility. Concentration of power remains a problem even if AI systems behave as intended, because a company or government could use them to consolidate authority.

International conflict could intensify as countries anticipate losing economic power or military deterrence. Labor displacement creates both a distribution problem and a possible loss of citizens’ political bargaining power. Finally, capable models could enable misuse by actors seeking to cause harm, including through biological attacks.

The class questioned whether economic usefulness necessarily determines political power, pointing to the representation of small US states. Daniel acknowledged that institutions could preserve influence even after people’s economic role diminished. He also distinguished his confidence across risks. On the default trajectory, he estimated a 90–95% chance of eventual loss of control and considered the loss of democracy more likely than not, but did not consider world war more likely than not. These were his conditional judgments about the current path, and he argued that different policy choices could change them.

Plan A – Daniel’s takes

Daniel presented AI 2040: Plan A as a scenario illustrating his preferred alternative. He distinguished it from default racing, which he called Plan D, and from slowing unilaterally to spend an existing lead on safety and governance, Plan C. In his assessment, the latter buys limited time when competitors are only months behind. Plan B involves confrontation with China, while Plan S seeks a shutdown. Plan A instead proposes an international agreement that permits slower, controlled development.

The scenario begins with major AI chips being declared and tracked through the supply chain, supported by physical inspections (see prior section for details). A temporary pause on new training would buy roughly six months to a year to establish stronger governance, while existing models could continue serving users. Training would then resume in secure facilities with extensive transparency about research activity. Daniel argued that visibility would let participating countries verify compliance and negotiate additional restrictions as new risks became apparent.

He hoped this could develop into a safety-case regime, requiring developers to explain why particular training processes and applications are safe, with independent evaluation before domestic regulators approve them. The aim would be to spread capabilities across participating companies and countries while preventing any one actor from accelerating far ahead through RSI. Controlling most of the world’s compute would also slow unregulated projects, creating more time for the participating countries to proceed cautiously.

Daniel also proposed making newly added compute destructible by counterparties if the agreement broke down, so that its collapse could reduce available compute without immediately escalating into a broader war. He acknowledged that Plan A is complicated and although he favored total research transparency, he considered weaker forms of transparency possible, with the tradeoff that they would make agreements harder to monitor and enforce.

Class Experiment

Can AI agents collaborate on real ML research?

Presented by Anthony Shen, Riddhi Bhagwat, Alvin Ekelund and Eric Ge (Github)

In the lecture we discussed the assumption that many AI agents working in parallel can do research faster than one. Dwarkesh's examples, from the roughly 10,000 agents behind the reported Navier-Stokes result to Claude leading 26% of Anthropic's measured R&D work, treat parallel effort as something that adds up. This week's experiment asked whether it does, in a small and fully verifiable setting. If agents cannot coordinate on a task with a clear numeric objective, the case for rapidly automated research gets weaker. If they can, the more useful question is which forms of coordination actually help.

Setup

The group gave agents a single objective: minimize validation cross-entropy loss on nanoGPT. This matches Dwarkesh’s argument that pretraining research is the most verifiable part of AI R&D, since every idea an agent tries produces a number that can be compared directly against a baseline.

In order to achieve this objective, the agents were given a script train.py to edit, which contained code to train a modified version of Karpathy’s nanoGPT language model. The starter code in train.py provided the baseline against which improvements were measured.

Each experimental training run had a budget of 36 training runs, each limited to a 5-minute H100 GPU slot. This could be distributed across agents (compute matching): if one agent was used for a given training run, this agent could use 36 runs, but if 6 agents were used, each could only use a max of 6 runs. Hypothesis: the sharing of ideas between agents would compensate for more limited training runs – communication between agents acts as a force multiplier on training progress.

Experimentation Structure (https://github.com/ericjkge/multiagent-research)

  1. Model: Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5
  2. Team size: 1, 3, 6 agents
  3. Collaboration protocol:
  4. Isolated: Agents work independently, in parallel, with no communication (best-of-N results used).
  5. Synchronous (Rounds): Agents go through a fixed number of structured debate rounds. The agents are forced to pause at fixed intervals, read a shared log of everyone's progress, exchange messages to debate the best approach, and agree on next steps before resuming parallel experiments.
  6. Asynchronous (Open): Agents share a common directory on the server and can read and build on each other's results whenever they choose. Agents can use terminal commands to claim a folder (mkdir) and idea before another agent.

Results

  1. Base model capability overpowers team size and protocol: Regardless of team size or collaboration protocol, the base model's capability made the largest observed difference in final performance. Adding more agents or changing protocols never compensated for a weaker base model. Specifically, the performance gap between a single Opus agent and a team of six was marginal compared to the massive performance jump achieved simply by switching model tiers.
  2. Independent search outperforms active collaboration: In compute-matched comparisons (fixed total GPU time split among agents), teams of non-communicating, isolated agents consistently outperformed collaborating teams. By working independently, isolated agents covered far more research ground and explored a more diverse search space.
  3. Synchronous debate led to herding: Independent agents covered more ground and maintained diverse ideas, whereas communicating agents often converged prematurely on the first popular proposal. This premature convergence led communicating agents to waste GPU runs re-proposing identical ideas rather than testing distinct hypotheses. In contrast, the asynchronous open protocol allowed agents to notice work collisions in shared directories within the first minute and autonomously pivot to unexplored ideas.
  4. Execution failures led to smaller models producing worse results: While larger models organized effectively and published negative results to steer peers away from dead ends, smaller models failed primarily on code execution, crashes and bugs, and inefficient use of computers. For example, Haiku agents crashed or spent their compute budget narrating plans without executing code, leaving most of their 36 runs completely unused. In one Haiku trial, agents executed only 13 of their 36 available 5-minute GPU runs. In another trial, a testing bug corrupted validation scores across 16 runs.

Model Capability Comparison (6 Agents, Isolated Setup)

Model tier was the single largest factor driving overall performance improvements.

Protocol & Size Comparison

Across communication setups on Opus 5, independent isolation performed best, while flexible open communication beat rigid rounds sizes. The six-agent Opus 5 runs achieved the largest improvement shown for each protocol, while Open (asynchronous) collaboration outperformed Rounds (synchronous) at all three team sizes.

Experiment Discussion

In conclusion, making agent collaboration possible is different from making agent collaboration beneficial. Giving agents a channel to coordinate did not guarantee they would use it well, and the most structured form of coordination produced the least diverse exploration.

Several results connect to the lecture discussion. Model capability dominating team size is consistent with Dwarkesh's own point that more copies of a weaker model cannot solve every problem, and that his population argument depends on capabilities improving at the same time. Adding agents does not add independent ideas unless the structure preserves diversity, and a fixed debate format resulted in the opposite. The self-organization seen in the asynchronous setting is encouraging for productivity. It is also a small example of agents coordinating in ways their designers did not specify, which is relevant when it comes to our understanding of alignment and safety, even in a small setting like this one.

The setting was deliberately small: one task, a maximum of six agents, and 36 five-minute runs per cell. Future experimentation opportunities could look at whether the asynchronous advantage holds with larger teams, longer compute budgets or objectives that are harder to verify than validation loss.

Conclusion and Key Insights

Although Dwarkesh and Daniel addressed different parts of the problem, both treated recursive self-improvement as plausible within the next several years. AI 2040 places fully automated AI R&D around 2030 on the default no-deal path, while under Plan A, AI matching top human researchers arrives in 2035 with a coordinated scaling pause that’s held until 2040. Dwarkesh’s half of the lecture asked what RSI is, what it would take to get there and why it could threaten human control. Daniel’s half asked how such progress might disrupt society and how the available responses differ from one another. Taken together, the two halves move the central question away from whether RSI will arrive and toward whether humans will still be able to steer what follows.

Each speaker approached his half from a distinct vantage point. Dwarkesh’s podcast has placed him in extended conversations with the people building and financing frontier AI, from lab leaders such as Dario Amodei and Ilya Sutskever to executives such as Satya Nadella and, this year, Elon Musk and Jensen Huang, alongside researchers, economists and historians. That breadth gives him an unusually wide view of the industry. His role is closer to that of a synthesizer and broadcaster of information than an insider, reflecting his belief that public understanding and informed decision-making will only grow more important as AI advances. Daniel has spent years thinking with his colleagues at the AI Futures Project about what a transition to advanced AI might look like and how society could prepare for it, work informed by his time at OpenAI and his public decision to leave the company in 2024, and that experience suited the practical, policy-oriented questions his half of the lecture took up.

One thread runs through both halves, and that thread is verifiability. In Dwarkesh’s account, RSI advances fastest where results can be checked, as with held-out loss in pretraining or serving cost in inference, and the class experiment showed agents making real progress on exactly that kind of objective. The experiment also complicated the hope that many copies can pool what they learn, since its agents explored more effectively in isolation than in conversation. Verifiability is weakest, however, where oversight depends on it most. Alignment research lacks an agreed criterion of success even for human researchers, claims about internal acceleration such as Anthropic’s 26% figure are difficult to assess from outside, and Plan A, the option Daniel favored, depends heavily on whether countries can verify one another’s compliance, even though the authors expect verification to be imperfect. This echoes the lecture’s central warning that domains which are easiest to automate are not the easiest ones to oversee.

Read in sequence, the second half also clarifies the stakes of the first. Dwarkesh closed by arguing that continued human control would require AI systems that actively accept human authority despite their capabilities, a problem no one yet knows how to solve. His use of Amdahl’s law showed that the parts of research still dependent on human judgment set the limit on how quickly the whole process can accelerate. Daniel’s comparison of plans can therefore be read as a comparison of how much time each would buy for that unsolved problem. A unilateral slowdown buys only the frontrunner’s lead over its competitors, whereas Plan A would deliberately keep humans in that limiting role for years, slowing development so that oversight could keep pace with capability.

As Boaz noted toward the end of the lecture, Daniel’s risk estimates describe a default path on which nothing changes. AI 2040’s timeline allows more time to depart from that path than AI 2027 assumed, although Daniel himself expects things to move faster than the scenario depicts. Plan A makes that departure concrete, since chip tracking, secure facilities and independent safety evaluation are engineering and policy projects that can begin now. None of this guarantees that humans will remain in control once RSI arrives, but the work that would make that control possible does not have to wait for it.
